title: Braving the Wilderness: The Quest for True Belonging and the Courage to Stand Alone
source_note: Book itself not read; summary sites partly blocked or paywalled. The belonging quote, BRAVING list and Integrity definition are from the author's knowledge of the book (high familiarity, not re-fetched). Collective joy and pain material is the lowest-confidence part.

facts.claim: The book (2017) is about true belonging and the courage to stand alone. Brown's wording: true belonging does not require us to change who we are; it requires us to be who we are. Belonging first needs belonging to ourselves.

Fitting in means conforming to other people's expectations, such as nodding along to avoid conflict; true belonging means feeling secure communicating and living out your values whatever others think.
Brown began writing herself permission slips; the first said 'you're allowed to be goofy, have fun, and enjoy life'.

The book's trust framework BRAVING: Boundaries, Reliability, Accountability, Vault, Integrity, Non-judgment, Generosity. Integrity is defined as choosing courage over comfort, choosing what is right over what is fun, fast or easy, and practicing your values, not just professing them.
facts.source: author knowledge; fourminutebooks lists reliable, own your mistakes, respect boundaries, be generous

facts.claim: Shortform lists strategies: resolve conflict with curiosity and boundaries, question false 'us versus them' dichotomies, remember what unites us by being present in joyful and painful moments, build trust in yourself and others.
Brown names three obstacles: lack of shared humanity, lack of compassion, fear of becoming an outsider.
Antoine Leiris's letter 'You Will Not Have My Hate', written after the November 2015 Paris attacks that killed 130, is used for the lesson of turning anger into betterness, not bitterness.

The book discusses collective joy and collective pain as ways people connect, with 'Hold hands. With strangers.' as one of four practices. The idea of collective effervescence (Durkheim) and Barbara Ehrenreich's Dancing in the Streets (group events with music, synchronised movement, costumes, loss of self; elites turn participants into spectators) lie behind it. That Brown cites Durkheim and Ehrenreich is from memory, not confirmed.
facts.source: author knowledge; Wikipedia: Dancing in the Streets

facts.claim: Brown sets Maya Angelou's idea that you are free when you realise you belong no place and every place, as the book's theme.

The other BRAVING elements as Brown describes them: Boundaries (respect what the other says is and is not okay; ask when unclear); Reliability (do what you say you will do); Accountability (own mistakes, apologize, make amends); Vault (do not share what is not yours to share); Non-judgment (each can ask for what they need and talk about feelings without judgment); Generosity (the most generous interpretation of others' intentions, words and actions).
